analysis.title: Global Economic Outlook: Shortened sails, shifting winds (Quarterly, extract)
key_insights: Global growth is moderating but not breaking. AI investment and private consumption sustain the expansion into 2027, while slower capex growth, high inflation and rates, and tighter fiscal support cap it. Central banks are closer to the end of tightening than the start of easing.

The central scenario is a narrowing path to a soft landing. It requires AI monetisation to be fast enough to fund capex but not so fast that it causes large layoffs, no financing squeeze on the non-AI economy, and contained political resistance. SG sees more ways for AI to go wrong than right, which means a fatter left tail.

Five 2027 scenarios are built from AI outcomes (capex holds, capex crashes, productivity delivers) and two oil paths. Risks lean toward stagflation rather than recession. Sharply lower oil with sustained AI capex gives a 'no landing' outcome.

An AI capex bust would be a major shock but not necessarily a systemic financial crisis, because banks are better capitalised and non-AI private balance sheets are healthier. Opaque project structures, circular financing and non-bank exposures obscure where losses would land.

Consensus hyperscaler capex is about $770bn in 2026 and above $1.1tn in 2027, growth of 87% and 49%. With half spent in the US, AI capex adds 0.6pp to US nominal GDP growth in 2026 and 0.5pp in 2027, so the incremental impulse fades from 2027 and more clearly from 2028.

US growth is forecast at 2.6% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027. Fiscal stimulus fades after the administration lost the House in the midterms, creating a mechanical payback in 2027. Growth in 1H27 should run below trend.

US inflation is persistent. Underlying PCE has been range-bound at 2.5-3%. Core PCE is forecast at about 3.3% in 2026 (Q4/Q4) and about 2.9% in 2027, and not persistently below 3% until October 2027. Delayed tariff and oil pass-through add to it.

SG expects two more 25bp Fed hikes, in December 2026 and March 2027, taking the terminal rate to 4.375%. Further hikes are possible if core PCE lingers near 3%. A policy-rule analysis puts the current funds rate below the level consistent with inflation and labour conditions.

The FOMC is described as split between gradualists, who expect core inflation momentum to slow, and officials who want tighter policy sooner. A possible revamp of the FOMC framework could matter more than the near-term rate path.

Euro area growth excluding Ireland is steady at about 1.0-1.1%. Net exports recover and domestic demand is resilient, while higher rates weigh mainly on housing investment, with the bulk of the GDP effect arriving in 2028.

Euro area headline inflation hit 4.0% yoy in October and is forecast to peak at 4.3-4.4% in early 2027. Core is forecast at about 2.8% in early 2027. Food inflation is forecast above 4% in 2H27. The 2027 headline forecast is 3.4%.

The ECB is expected to hike in December and then pause, with a terminal rate of 2.75% and risks skewed to further hikes in 2027. Markets price a higher terminal rate than the economists' consensus. Lagarde steps down on 7 February 2027.

The ECB bar for intervening in sovereign bond stress is high. No spread level triggers action (Italian spreads reached 300bp in 2018 without action). If needed, TPI, OMT, temporary asset purchases or LTROs could be used, conditional on credible corrective fiscal action by the affected government.

France is the top European event risk. SG expects fiscal consolidation to be the endgame whoever wins the 2027 presidential election, but spreads should stay volatile and high until credibility is established. Le Pen polls around 35% and is the favourite, and Moody's surprise rating hold on 23 October was noted.

Spain votes on 29 November and polls favour a PP-Vox government (PP 130 seats, Vox 65, 176 needed for a majority). That would mean tighter fiscal policy and immigration, and a faster drop in domestic demand pressure. Italy's Meloni is the favourite for 2027 but the race is competitive, and an early spring election is possible.

China is expected to see policy stabilise but not rebalance growth. Reflation is unlikely, with a 'high production, weak demand' model persisting. SG expects a 2027 GDP target of about 4.5% and growth shifting from exports to policy-backed investment. A nationwide home-price bottom is not expected until 2028.

The BoJ is expected to hike in December, March and June to a 2% terminal rate. Upside risk exists if the US 10-year yield stays above 5%, which could keep USD/JPY at 157-159 and push the terminal rate above 2%. Hawkish board members Takata and Tamura retire in July 2027.

The UK is expected to get one final 25bp BoE hike in February to 4.25%. Labour slack is judged enough to limit second-round wage effects, but wage growth of about 3.5% is above target-consistent levels. UK fiscal consolidation is doubted by markets, and the UK has the highest 10-year yields in the G7.

Emerging markets are expected to hold up. Inflation persistence has not broadly increased (only Nigeria shows strong evidence), but policy buffers have eroded since June as currencies weakened and global yields rose. Korea is the main exception with room to ease, while Brazil and Colombia are the most vulnerable on debt.

Brazil: after Lula's surprise runoff win, 10-year yields rose to 15.2% and the BRL fell 12%, the worst EM currency this quarter. Gross debt is 82.9% of GDP and the 2027 package of BRL43-54bn of savings falls short of the BRL70-80bn that markets wanted.

El Niño should amplify food inflation but have a muted growth effect. The World Bank expects global food commodity prices to rise about 18% cumulatively over 2026-27, or 30% in an adverse case. Energy, not El Niño, is the main driver, and India, Indonesia and South Africa face the largest growth downside.

R-star (the neutral rate) is judged higher than in the 2010s, driven by fiscal needs and capital-intensive AI, energy and security investment. Estimates are model-dependent and should be treated as a range. Central banks are behind the curve against the midpoint of that range.

Oil is assumed to stay around $90-100/bbl, with Brent easing to about $85 by end-2027. The baseline for the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars is frozen conflict. Crude rose about 30% between August and October after the Iran conflict flared up again.

Taiwan and Korea are the most exposed to a slowdown in AI capex. AI-related exports are about 50% of GDP in Taiwan and 12% in Korea. A gradual slowdown is judged manageable, while a disorderly credit-led bust would hit economies with weaker balance sheets harder.

EU-China tensions are a growing 2027 risk. EU safeguard measures on chemicals, furniture and machinery may come in 1Q27, and China's rare earth licensing truce expires in January 2027. A full trade war is judged a tail risk.

risk_factors: AI capex disappointment, financing strain, political or regulatory backlash, or supply-chain fragmentation.
Stagflation if an AI capex slowdown coincides with expensive oil.
Fresh energy or supply shocks arriving before earlier inflation pressures clear, and entrenching medium-term inflation expectations.
El Niño and energy-driven food inflation, with effects potentially extending into early 2028.
A US 10-year yield above 5% keeping the yen weak and forcing the BoJ above 2%.
French fiscal and political stress, with spread volatility until after the 2027 elections.
K-shaped consumption: spending retrenchment if an asset-price correction hits affluent households or labour income weakens.
Concentrated EM vulnerabilities in Brazil, Colombia, South Africa and Hungary from higher global yields and a strong dollar.
Opaque, concentrated AI-related losses in non-bank and private-market exposures.
geopolitical: Iran-US war and Russia-Ukraine war: SG's baseline is frozen conflict with persistent supply-chain disruption keeping oil elevated, and escalation risk remains.
EU-China trade tensions: DiversifyEU proposal due December 2026, possible EU safeguards on chemicals, furniture and machinery in 1Q27, and the rare earth licensing truce expiring January 2027.
US chip export controls and AI supply-chain fragmentation could widen the US technology lead and strengthen China's push for domestic chips.
European elections in Spain (29 November), France (April-June 2027), Italy and Poland could shift EU governance to the right and make it more fragmented.
Brazil's presidential runoff victory by Lula raised fiscal credibility concerns.

tension_points.bull_case: Sustained AI investment with strong cloud revenue growth keeps capex a major growth engine in 2027, adding about 0.5pp to US nominal GDP growth. Productivity gains broaden and hyperscaler cash flows fund the build-out.
tension_points.bear_case: Investment commitments outrun realised returns, leverage expands and financing tightens. Political and regulatory backlash or supply-chain fragmentation delay projects, and a telecom-style reversal could spread through trade and household wealth.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Failure of any of three conditions: AI monetisation fast enough to keep investors funding capex, no material tightening of non-AI credit conditions, and contained political resistance. A sharp slowdown in capex growth in coming quarters is the test.

tension_points.bull_case: Gradualists expect core inflation momentum to slow as tariff and energy shocks fade, which would limit hikes to the two SG expects.
tension_points.bear_case: Underlying PCE stuck at 2.5-3% and delayed tariff and oil pass-through point to structurally high core inflation, which could require more hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: November and later inflation data released after the December meeting: if annual core PCE inflation looks likely to linger around 3% into 2027, SG sees notably higher risk of hikes beyond March.

tension_points.bull_case: Long-term inflation expectations settle near 2% in 2027, and a 2% terminal rate steers USD/JPY toward about ¥150.
tension_points.bear_case: Persistently high US yields keep the yen weak and force the BoJ above 2%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A US 10-year yield remaining above 5% would keep USD/JPY from falling to ¥150 even at a 2% policy rate.
